title: Basic Human Goodness - Buddha Nature
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up basic human goodness, which is Buddha nature, against the backdrop of the COVID-19 fall surge. Kanho opens with a prayer for essential workers by dharma sister Sean Evans, then turns to impermanence and the Western sense of original sin and shame, set beside the Zen view that problems are temporary defilements covering basic goodness. Generosity follows, with the emptiness of giver, receiver and gift and a short poem of Kanho's own. Kanho then thanks postal workers, grocery and farm workers, and hospital staff, and reads names of doctors and nurses who have died, ending with the four bodhisattva vows.

sentences.text: Thank you very much for having patience with all my fumbling and switching screens and miscues.
Thank you for your generosity.
I apologize upfront: my talk is going to be a little longer than they usually are.
There was so much I wanted to say, and my apologies if it is too long.
An additional apology, because I included a poem that I wrote, and I've got to tell you right now, I am the poet.
So thank you.
Thank you.
Good evening, and thank you for being here.
It's challenging in these times to show up, and I have one question.
Ken, are you recording?
Thank you.
It's hard to show up because let us look at what's going on right now.

Social unrest, love, generosity, political strife, practice commitments, sacrifice, beauty, turning seasons, a global pandemic, sangha, sunrises, the COVID-19 fall surge, children are being born, people are dying.
It is all one happening, one world.
Some of it we find pleasant, some of it we would like to avoid.
But how can we chase after one and reject the other?
There is no turning away, for it is all one world.
Events and people are tightly braided together into one whole.
I would like to begin this talk with a prayer by my dharma sister, Sean Evans.
The prayer is called a prayer for all essential workers.
*For all the essential bodhisattvas who are hearing and responding to the cries of the whole world.
For all the postal workers touching and delivering our mail.
For all the grannies and aunties and neighbors and daycare guardians who are secretly caring for our little children at home, while their essential worker parents must go to work.

For all the EMTs and ambulance caregivers, for the firefighters and police, all the drivers transporting and receiving us, protecting our brothers and sisters and children and parents, our grandparents, our newborns, our homeless, our beloved, our friends.
Prayers, prayers, and more prayers.
For the women and men in hospital basements, laundering sheets and blankets for those who are sick and dying.
For the essential cooks and kitchen helpers who continuously feed and nourish everyone.
For the floor washers, the garbage collectors, the ones who clean up our mess.*
*Prayers to the brave keepers and tenders of bodies, the grave diggers, the funeral workers, the ones who accompany the dead.
Prayers for the subway and bus conductors, the pharmacists, the food store cashiers, the essential unloaders of all boxes and crates.
For all the school teachers offering their lesson plans and their love to students online so they can continue with their current education and not fall behind.
For all the maintenance workers, truckers, line workers, and food processors.
For all the crop pickers and packers.
For all the public health workers tracing and contacting, testing, and reporting, doing their jobs despite heavy caseloads, despite improper tools or clear leadership.
Many prayers for the very essential Dr.
Anthony Fauci.
For all the physicians, nurses, social workers, and care technicians who carry on despite the challenges.
Prayers.
Many, many prayers.
So many prayers for so many.
For all the essential workers, seen and unseen, watching over and holding all of us all the time.
Essential bodhisattvas arising in all ten directions, hearing and responding to our cries in this pandemic world through all space and time.*
So tonight, I would like to speak of basic human goodness, which is Buddha nature, and all these heroes in unexpected places.
Because all these essential workers are heroes.
I would like to speak of all things, no matter what they are, because they are as they are.
They can't be any other way.
And what they are is Buddha, the absolute reality beyond good and evil.
Bodhisattva vows move us toward and commit us to caring for everyone's short-term and long-term benefit, both physical and spiritual.
We can cultivate this vow, and our practice is to strengthen and extend it.
We wish enlightenment for all beings, all beings, including ourselves, including the people we find despicable or not so likable.

At the same time, I don't know about you, but I am saddened, angry, moved in awe, witnessing and connected to the events now taking place in the streets of our cities, in our hospitals, in our government.
At times I feel uplifted, and sometimes I am overwhelmed by what is going on.
Fortunately, our practice helps us to work with all this.
We can rely on impermanence and basic goodness.
As practitioners, we have always understood that impermanence is a cornerstone of Buddhist teaching and practice.
All that exists is impermanent.
Nothing lasts and nothing can be grasped or held onto.
Please let me repeat: this teaching of impermanence is essential to our practice.
When we don't fully appreciate this simple but profound truth, we suffer deeply.
When we do accept the reality of impermanence, we can have peace and understanding.
As far as classical Buddhism is concerned, impermanence is the number one inescapable and essentially painful fact of life.
It is an existential problem that Buddhist practice is meant to address.
We cannot turn away from that which is difficult, and we must make a continuous effort to turn toward it.
To understand impermanence at the deepest possible level and to merge with it fully is the Buddhist path.
Everything we like and everything we dislike will change.
We all understand this on a superficial level, but it is very worthwhile to go deeper and understand it in our heart.
The world today seems filled with evil at times.
In truth, however, there have always been great upheavals, great struggles in one part of the world or another.
No doubt, people felt the same way during the plague or in 1918 during the Spanish flu.
They have felt like this in Nazi Germany, under Russian Tsars, under any regime where people felt oppressed.
How could a reasonable, scientific, enlightened, and progressive culture tolerate wars, genocide, ignore mass starvation, and a race toward more and more powerful weapons?
In the meantime, the planet is heating up and humanity can't seem to find the political will to do anything about it.
In fact, collectively, we all turn up the heat.
And yet, our Zen tradition believes in human goodness, that every sentient being has Buddha nature, while Western religious ideas seem to be pervaded by original sin and shame.
Actually, this attitude seems to run through Western thought in general.
I read that among patients and therapists alike, there seems to be a continuous struggle of some original mistake, which causes all the suffering as a punishment.
A sense of guilt or being wounded is a frequent undercurrent, along with blame and shame.
Let us recognize that these are temporary, habitual patterns that develop based on the environment and society and past experience.
Through practice, we can see through all these obstacles, and we can extend our compassion to all beings.
In a more Buddhist perspective, while there may be many problems, they are temporary and superficial defilements that cover over one's basic goodness.
When we sit long enough, we can often see the tangles that create these conditions and outcomes we consider negative.
This basic goodness is also called Buddha nature or Tathagata Garbha.
This viewpoint is a life-affirming, positive, and optimistic one.
And it is important to realize that this viewpoint is not purely conceptual.
It is rooted in our own experience of meditation and sangha.
I really struggled putting this together, so let me put this differently and in slightly different words.
Zen practice is different from the mistake mentality.
The mind is fundamentally pure, healthy, and positive.
Problems are temporary and superficial defilements.
We cannot get rid of problems, but we can shift the focus.
Problems seen in a much broader context, and then we can begin to let go of clinging to our conditioning.
We can begin to step beyond obsession and identification with our stories.
The emphasis is no longer on the problems, but rather on the ground of experience through realizing the nature of mind itself.
Basic goodness doesn't imply good over bad in relative terms.
Humans and society as a whole have basic goodness.
How would our life change if we could take on that outlook?
I encourage us all to investigate this question with curiosity.
We humans come into the world holding our Buddha nature, and we are wired for basic goodness.
When we engage in practices that are designed to cultivate kindness and compassion, we're not actually creating something new that didn't already exist.
What we're doing is recognizing and strengthening a quality that was there from the outset.
This leap in faith may seem rather radical.
We can, however, transform our fear into faith in human goodness, and we can transform the tightness of our rage and anger into generosity and love.
Our guide instructs us to begin by giving vegetable greens or other little things, that later, step by step, the habit once acquired, we may be able to donate our very flesh.
Here comes the difficult question: how do we practice with that?
How does this kind of giving become part of our life, our Bodhisattva path?
Because there are no automatic saints who help the downtrodden masses.
In fact, there are no saints and no masses.
One little blip in the flow of the universe, and all roles could be reversed.
Unearned privilege, luck of the draw.
And generosity itself is grounded in the reality of the emptiness of the three wheels of giver, receiver and gift.
We receive and we give our life.
One little warning about generosity: it is easily tainted.
We can become prideful in giving, and then duality creeps back in.
And when it does, and it will, we do know how to cut the strings to the gift.
Being generous, being in love, is not a transaction, not part of a barter system.
We cannot buy love through gifts.
Pure generosity is simply giving and forgetting.
The empty hand offers an empty gift to an empty receiver.
Just this.
Just gratitude.
Simply giving is enough.
Now, as warned at the very beginning, comes a brief poem of mine.
*Breathing, laughing, I throw my life like a net.
I haul and gather, always.
It brings back enough.
Seeing, smiling with closed eyes, I scatter my harvest.
Freely given, it is not my concern anymore.
Reading, dreaming, I wonder about merit.
If there's good and bad, and if maybe not being blind to causality is enough.*
*Hoping, waiting, I long for the future of poverty and Zen, with no distinction between me and the whole universe.
Giving, living, all the gifts left along the way.
Multiply and return, and nothing is more than enough.*
Generosity expresses itself, or we express generosity.
It shows up in all different ways.
It arises in the heart, mind, body, that is in the middle of a field of lived experience, environmental, relational, social, and cultural.
Generosity can be seen as an emergent process, as becoming prominent in a relationship between body, mind, and the environment.
And being generous, we enact a role.
We change the world, and in turn, we are changed by this world.
Now, I would like to speak of generosity and of heroes in unexpected places, of essential workers, of generous beings.
For every person that orders that mail is slowed down and that sorting machines are destroyed, there are probably five or ten who sabotage that order.
We say thank you.
For every political appointee, there are many in civil service who care for their institutions and try to make things work.
We say thank you.
People go to work so we can go shopping, so we can put food on our table.
We say thank you.
The people working at the banks and the gas stations so we can fill up our cars with gas.
We say thank you.
The guy in front of Trader Joe's who hands out masks and disinfects the shopping carts.
We say thank you.
The agricultural workers who, often under poor conditions, harvest and process our food.
We say thank you.
Fire and police departments, we say thank you.
Let us breathe for a minute with this.
Now let me speak of the generosity of those who staff our hospitals, the ambulance drivers, the doctors and nurses, the lab techs.
We say thank you.
They are on the front lines to help the rest of us.
We say thank you.
A nurse may hold the hand of our loved one as they are dying because we are not allowed to be there.
We say thank you.
And they are dying for us, more than a thousand of them already.
Each one of them knows that their life is in danger and they go back to work.
We say thank you.
Here are some of the names.
I apologize for any mispronunciations.
Starting at A, ending at C, and leaving out the middle thousand.
*Isaac Abadi, MD, 84, founder, professor of internal medicine and rheumatology.
Escuela de Medicina Luis Rosetti, Hospital Universitario de Caracas, Caracas, Venezuela.
Musafat Abadi, age unknown, emergency medicine specialist in Tehran, Iran.
Lynn Ann Abadzenen, 43, Neonatology, Philippine General Hospital, Metro Manila, Philippines.*
*Abdullah Abbasi, 65, infectious disease specialist, Gorgon, Iran.
Mohammad Abdelbazed El-Jabiri, age unknown, infectious disease specialist in Baba Fibers Hospital, Egypt.
Tilmatin Abdenour, 60, general medicine, EPSP, Pujnafa, Sidi, Mohamed, Algiers, Algeria.*
1,000 more names.
*Jack Zoller, 91, OB-GYN, New Orleans, Louisiana.
Rosabco, 71, post anesthesia care unit.
NYSNA member, St.
Joseph Hospital, Bethphage, New York.
Ricardo Zucco, age unknown, neurologist, Italy.*
*Lani Zuniga, 53, nurse, Surrey Hills Nursing Home, Godalming, Surrey, England.
Roger Malkiel Zunza-Maiti, age unknown, nurse, UMAE Hospital de Alta Especialidad Merida, Yucatan, Mexico.
Baron Jacobus Jimmy Sweep, 67, family medicine, general practitioner, Medi-Cross, Princess Crossing, Road Port, South Africa.*
We thank you.
May our intention equally extend to every being and place, with the true merit of Buddha's way.
*Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are endless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.*
